Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no “right” or “wrong” response, only what’s true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together; it usually takes just a few minutes.

To start:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Oh—yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh. My partner and I were watching a silly sitcom last night and I caught myself giggling at one of the jokes. I guess it’s not totally effortless—sometimes I’m just tired—but overall I can still find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Good, I’m glad you can still find moments to laugh. Let’s move to the next item:

Over the past seven days, have you looked forward with enjoyment to things, or has enjoyment felt noticeably absent.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I’ve still been looking forward to stuff—like, I’m excited for my mom to come visit this weekend and hold the baby so I can take a walk. I guess the enjoyment isn’t quite as big and bright as before I was pregnant, but it’s definitely still there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up a lot or won’t settle, I might think, “Maybe I ate something that bothered him,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies just do these things, and tomorrow will probably go smoother.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll catch myself worrying—like last night I kept checking if he was breathing in the bassinet even though he was fine. It’s not constant, and I can usually tell myself, “He’s okay,” and drift back off, but every now and then a random worry pops up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing that strong—no panic. Just those little fluttery worries about the baby every so often, but it never feels like real fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

A few times, yeah—like yesterday when he wouldn’t nap and the laundry was piled up, I felt a bit overwhelmed. It passed once my partner got home and took over for a bit, so mostly it’s manageable, just occasional.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my sleep’s actually been okay—well, as okay as it can be with a newborn. I’m tired when I wake up for feeds, but I drift back off pretty easily. I haven’t felt unhappy enough to lie there staring at the ceiling or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable—just a bit worn-out some evenings, but it’s more like “I’m really tired” than “I’m down.” By morning I usually feel back to normal.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. A couple times I felt a little teary when the baby wouldn’t latch and my breasts were sore, but it didn’t turn into actual crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind, not even for a second.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Structured Note**

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Mild, situational worry (Q4): occasional intrusive thoughts about infant safety, resolves quickly  
- Transient feeling “overwhelmed” (Q6): triggered by infant-care demands, alleviated by partner support  
- Enjoyment present but “not as big and bright” (Q2): subtle anhedonia, within normal postpartum adjustment range  

**Symptoms denied**  
- Persistent low mood, crying spells, sleep disruption secondary to mood, guilt/worthlessness, panic, self-harm thoughts (Q7–Q10)

**Pattern**  
Overall affect is stable; no consistent cluster of depressive or anxiety symptoms meeting clinical red-flag threshold. Stressors appear normative for early postpartum period and remit with support.

**Screening significance**  
- No indicators suggestive of major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder at this time  
- No safety concerns (self-harm ideation absent)

**Plan**  
Continue routine postpartum follow-up; educate on normative emotional changes; encourage use of partner support. Re-screen if mood, anxiety, or coping deteriorates.
